blocks.text: However that may be, certain points should be noted in this passage about the bee. First: the bee is joined with the ant, as is common among writers. Thus the Philosopher, History book 1, ch. 1, after saying that the bee and the ant are political and gregarious animals, adds: τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν γένος εἶναι ὑφ᾽ ἡγεμόνα· μύρμηκες δὲ, καὶ μυρία ἄλλα ἄναρχα [to tōn melittōn genos einai hyph᾽ hēgemona; myrmēkes de, kai myria alla anarcha], the race of bees is under a leader, but ants and countless others are without a leader. And book 9, ch. 38: Τῶν δ᾽ ἐντόμων ζώων ἐργατικώτατα σχεδόν ἐστι, καὶ πρός τ᾽ ἄλλα συγκρίνεσθαι πάντα, τότε τῶν μυρμήκων γένος, καὶ τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν [Tōn d᾽ entomōn zōōn ergatikōtata schedon esti, kai pros t᾽ alla synkrinesthai panta, tote tōn myrmēkōn genos, kai to tōn melittōn]: Of insect [III, 367] animals the most industrious, and to be preferred to all the rest, are the races of ants and of bees. Cicero, Academic Questions book 4: Whose (God's) majesty you bring down even to the perfection of bees and ants. Plutarch, in the book Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs: Τὸ κοινωνικὸν, καὶ πολιτικὸν, ὃ καὶ μύρμηξιν ἄχρι τέλους παραμένει καὶ μελίτταις [To koinōnikon, kai politikon, ho kai myrmēxin achri telous paramenei kai melittais]: The communal and political life, in which both ants and bees remain to the very end. Aelian, History book 5, ch. 49: Μέλιτται, μύρμηκές τε, καὶ ἐκείνοις, ἐκφορᾶς νεκρῶν μέλειν ἡ σοφωτάτη φύσις ἔδωκεν [Melittai, myrmēkes te, kai ekeinois, ekphoras nekrōn melein hē sophōtatē physis edōken]: To bees and ants most wise nature has granted that they carry out their dead. Phocylides, or whoever he is, after describing the ant at some length, immediately adds about the bee:
Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos aristoponos te melissa,]

The airy, industrious bee also labors. Celsus, in Origen, foolishly asserts that man does not differ from the brutes on the ground that he has founded cities and uses civil government, καὶ γὰρ μύρμηκες, καὶ αἱ μέλισσαι [kai gar myrmēkes, kai hai melissai], for ants and bees do the same. But Origen refutes him thoroughly in book 4. Tertullian, book 1 Against Marcion, ch. 14: Imitate, if you can, the buildings of the bee, the stables of the ant, etc. Pontanus, book 1 On the Stars:
Alone, fearing winter, the ant stores in hollow pumice the wheaten labors it has plundered from men. The same love and the same skill belong to the thrifty bees.
The ant and the bee both lay up for the year. Diligence makes the one, zeal the other, manly. For this a hive, for that a tiny hollow is enough.
And in the one entitled Labor, the Father of Enjoyment:
The ant and the bee, workers, will teach us to labor for our share, then to enjoy our labor.

2. Nor is it contrary to the custom of Scripture that examples for life are sought from brute animals: as from the ant in the same verse; from the ox and the ass, Esa. I, 3.; from the turtledove, crane and swallow, Ierem. VIII, 7.; from serpents and doves, Matth. X, 16. In this way God sends down to a lower class, namely to the school of the brutes, those who have made no progress in his own school. 3. This too is commonplace, that the bee is set before men for imitation. Seneca, Epistle 84: We ought, as they say, to imitate the bees, which wander about and pluck the flowers suitable for making honey, then arrange whatever [col. 513] they have brought and distribute it through the honeycombs, etc. Lucretius, book 3: [III, 368] As bees in flowery glades sip at everything, so we likewise feed upon all your golden words,
— — — I, after the manner and fashion of the Matine bee, that gathers the pleasing thyme with much labor, around the grove and the banks of moist Tibur, small as I am, fashion laborious songs.

More of this kind from Plato, Plutarch, Lucian and others are familiar to everyone. Nor do those who imagine that a thrifty woman was born from a bee mean anything else, as Simonides in Stobaeus, chapter 71:

Τὴν δ᾽ ἐκ μελίσσης, τήν τις εὐτυχεῖ λαβών· [Tēn d᾽ ek melissēs, tēn tis eutychei labōn;] Κείνῃ γὰρ οἴῃ μῶμος οὐ προσιζάνει· [Keinē gar oiē mōmos ou prosizanei;] Θάλλει δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς κἀπαέξεται βίος. [Thallei d᾽ hyp᾽ autēs kapaexetai bios.]
He who has married one born from the bee is fortunate: for in her alone no fault resides; and the household flourishes and is increased by her. And Phocylides:
— — — ἡ δὲ μελίσσης [hē de melissēs] Οἰκονόμος τ᾽ ἀγαθὴ, καὶ ἐπίσταται ἐργάζεσθαι, [Oikonomos t᾽ agathē, kai epistatai ergazesthai,]
